entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2023-0069: sudo-rs: Path Traversal vulnerability
entry.content:
sudo-rs: Path Traversal vulnerability

Aliases: CVE-2023-42456, GHSA-2r3c-m6v7-9354

Severity: CVSS_V3: CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:H/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L

Affected:

  • sudo-rs — fixed in 0.2.1

## Impact An issue was discovered where usernames containing the . and / characters could result in the corruption of specific files on the filesystem. As usernames are generally not limited by the characters they can contain, a username appearing to be a relative path can be constructed. For example we could add a user to the system containing the username ../../../../bin/cp. When logged in as a user with that name, that user could run sudo -K to clear their session record file. The session code then constructs the path to the session file by concatenating the username to the session file storage directory, resulting in a resolved path of /bin/cp. The code then clears that file, resulting in the cp binary effectively being removed from the system. An attacker needs to be able to login as…

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0344: Decompression bomb in `ruzstd`: a tiny input can exhaust memory (OOM)
entry.content:
Decompression bomb in `ruzstd`: a tiny input can exhaust memory (OOM)

Severity: CVSS_V3: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

Affected:

  • ruzstd — fixed in 0.9.1

A crafted `.zst` input under 128 KB can force `ruzstd` to allocate several gigabytes at once, crashing the process with an out-of-memory condition. Since `ruzstd` is a decoder for untrusted input, a single small file is enough to take down anything decoding it. The compressed size of a block was capped at 128 KB, but a compressed block's **decompressed** size was never checked against `Block_Maximum_Size = min(Window_Size, 128 KiB)` (RFC 8878). In `execute_sequences` the output was built with no running bound and no flush between blocks, so one block could expand to gigabytes — bypassing both the configured window-size limit and the block-by-block streaming that would otherwise release memory. (A related `u32` counter overflow on such a block caused an additional panic.) This is a denial…

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2021-0158: XSS in ammonia via SVG `animateMotion`, `animateTransform`, and/or `animateColor` tags
entry.content:
XSS in ammonia via SVG `animateMotion`, `animateTransform`, and/or `animateColor` tags

Aliases: GHSA-f2pc-rwv3-69mv

Affected:

  • ammonia — fixed in 4.1.7, 4.2.3

The neutralization that ammonia applied to `animate` and `set` was not applied to other forms of SVG animation, which can be used for XSS. The following SVG will produce a link with a javascript scheme. If the user clicks this link, they will run it. ```xml <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"> <a> <animateMotion attributeName="href" to="javascript:alert('SET_XSS')"></animateMotion> <text y="30">Click set</text> </a> </svg> ``` Ammonia did not apply attribute filters based on `attributeName`, so the contents of the `to`, `from`, and `values` tags were not sanitized as URLs. Applications that do not explicitly allow any of these tags should not be affected, since none are allowed by default. --- This vulnerability was reported by [ucsurf](https://uc.surf).

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0185: Remote memory exhaustion in quinn-proto from unbounded out-of-order stream reassembly
entry.content:
Remote memory exhaustion in quinn-proto from unbounded out-of-order stream reassembly

Aliases: CVE-2026-25800, GHSA-4w2j-m93h-cj5j

Severity: CVSS_V3: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

Affected:

  • quinn-proto — fixed in 0.11.15

The `Assembler` component that assembles unordered stream fragments into consecutive chunks of the stream incurs some overhead for non-contiguous fragments. Readers that read from a RecvStream in order (through an `AsyncRead` impl for example) will be sensitive to peers that send fragments while leaving out early parts of the stream, and in particular, fragments with many gaps (because these cannot be defragmented). In such a scenario, the receiving connection suffers from high buffer overhead, enabling memory exhaustion.

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0338: Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads
entry.content:
Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads

Aliases: GHSA-465w-v9q3-7j98

Affected:

  • quinn-proto — fixed in 0.11.18

When a stream is read in unordered mode (for example through `RecvStream::read(false)` in quinn-proto or `read_unordered` in `quinn`), quinn-proto proactively deduplicates received data by recording received ranges in a `RangeSet` through its `replace` method. When an incoming STREAM frame carried an empty payload, the `Drop` implementation of the iterator returned by `replace` inserted an empty range into the set, violating the invariant that stored ranges are non-empty. Subsequent frames overlapping that region then caused a panic while processing the stream. A remote peer can trigger this with five small STREAM frames (two of them zero-length) once the application has put the stream in unordered-read mode. The default ordered read path is not affected. The flaw was corrected in 0.11.1…

Aliases: GHSA-69v2-w9vg-4g83

  • ammonia — fixed in 4.1.7, 4.2.3

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0342: Zero-length DATAGRAM frames bypass the receive buffer limit in quinn-proto
entry.content:
Zero-length DATAGRAM frames bypass the receive buffer limit in quinn-proto

Aliases: GHSA-2hv7-gw8g-gpq5

Affected:

  • quinn-proto — fixed in 0.11.17

entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0240: Ed25519 identity public keys permit universal signature forgery
entry.content:
Ed25519 identity public keys permit universal signature forgery

Aliases: GHSA-7j32-2mpw-c784

Affected:

  • dcrypt-sign — fixed in 2.0.0

All published versions of `dcrypt-sign` before 2.0.0 accepted the Edwards identity as an Ed25519 public key. A signature with `R = B` and `S = 1` then verified for every message because the challenge term multiplied the identity. The implementation also admitted other noncanonical or small-order inputs. Consumers that accepted externally supplied dcrypt Ed25519 keys may therefore have accepted forged authorizations. Version 2.0.0 replaces the custom arithmetic with `ed25519-dalek`, uses strict verification, and rejects noncanonical, small-order, and non-torsion-free public keys and `R` values, as well as noncanonical `S >= L`. entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0242: Safe ErrorRegistry APIs can cause undefined behavior
entry.content:
Safe ErrorRegistry APIs can cause undefined behavior

Aliases: GHSA-7hc7-h3f2-r4j6

Affected:

  • dcrypt-api — fixed in 2.0.0

All published versions of `dcrypt-api` before 2.0.0 exposed safe `ErrorRegistry` operations that could trigger undefined behavior when the default `std` feature was enabled. entry.title: [UPDATED] RUSTSEC-2026-0238: Low-level GCM ignores the operation nonce
entry.content:
Low-level GCM ignores the operation nonce

Aliases: GHSA-h9f2-fgp8-vc4h

Affected:

  • dcrypt-algorithms — fixed in 2.0.0

In all published versions of `dcrypt-algorithms` before 2.0.0, the low-level `Gcm` builder required an operation nonce but derived `J0` from the nonce captured by the original `Gcm` constructor. Multiple operations could therefore silently reuse a nonce even when callers supplied distinct values, compromising confidentiality and authenticity under an affected key. Version 2.0.0 makes `Gcm` key-only and passes the operation nonce through IV derivation, encryption, and decryption. It also corrects non-96-bit IV processing, rejects tags shorter than 96 bits, and enforces counter limits. Applications must upgrade, identify affected keys, rotate them, and re-encrypt affected data; updating the implementation cannot restore security after nonce reuse.

In the ckb sync protocol, SyncState maintains a HashMap called 'misbehavior' that keeps a score of a peer's violations of the protocol. This HashMap is keyed to PeerIndex (an alias for SessionId), and entries are never removed from it. SessionId is an integer that increases monotonically with every new connection. A remote attacker can manipulate this HashMap to grow forever, resulting in degraded performance and ultimately a panic on allocation failure or being killed by the OS, depending on the platform. This impacts all versions of the crate before `2.5.0` back to `1.0.5`. Before version `1.0.5` the function that produces the iterator was broken to the point of being useless.
